question: Why the Mona Lisa is famous
title_suggestion: Why The Mona Lisa Is Famous? Facts, Myths and Evidence
h1: Why The Mona Lisa Is Famous?

sources.title: Portrait de Lisa Gherardini, épouse de Francesco del Giocondo, dit La Joconde ou Monna Lisa
notes: Catalogue identifies sitter as Lisa Gherardini, wife of Francesco del Giocondo, and dates the painting to 1503–1519.
Oil painting on poplar wood rather than canvas; the board has warped and cracked.
Leonardo retained the painting and likely it passed to Francis I around 1518.
The catalogue describes infrared examinations, later yellowed varnish and the fragility of the support.

sources.title: From the 'Mona Lisa' to 'The Wedding Feast at Cana' - The Salle des États
notes: Louvre explains subtle glazing and sfumato, enigmatic smile and sitter's turning pose.
Painting has occupied Salle des États since 1966; climate-controlled protective display responds to safety and poplar-panel conservation.
The painting's celebrity determines visitor experience and exhibition setting.

sources.title: Stolen: How the Mona Lisa Became the World’s Most Famous Painting
sources.author: James Zug
notes: The painting was stolen from the Louvre on 21 August 1911, leading to exceptional press coverage.
Historical reputation among critics preceded the theft, but mass public recognition was much less widespread.
The theft and recovery illustrate amplification of an established artistic reputation, not the creation of artistic merit.

sources.title: A superstar… and a wedding crowd!
notes: Museum identifies artistic execution, expression, landscape and sfumato as sources of the painting's appeal.
Louvre connects incidents including the 1911 theft with additional celebrity and gives context for prominent Salle des États display.

sources.title: The Mona Lisa in virtual reality in your own home
notes: Louvre's Beyond the Glass VR project contextualizes Lisa Gherardini and Leonardo's techniques.
The Louvre distinguishes historical curatorial reconstruction from the actual present-day exhibition and reflects the difficulty of face-to-face viewing.

verified_findings: The painterly technique and extraordinary later celebrity are different explanatory questions.
The 1911 theft magnified public attention to a painting already esteemed by specialists.
The identity of the sitter is firmly supported by the Louvre catalogue, despite persistent popular alternatives.
Conservation constraints are caused in part by the poplar panel, not merely by the painting's commercial or cultural value.
uncertainties: The relative contribution of critical reputation, theft, popular reproduction and tourism cannot be assigned a defensible percentage.
Museum display photographs and collection scans are not automatically licensed for reuse; individual asset rights still require checking.

plan: Dedicated original editorial hero contrasting painterly portrait detail with modern museum attention, without copying a protected photograph
Original diagram explaining the sfumato transition without representing it as an authentic Leonardo fragment
Timeline of critical esteem, 1911 theft, recovery and modern exhibition
Original explanatory panel on the poplar support and conservation constraints
